title: Professional boundaries, gifts and social media
blurb: Keep clear boundaries with patients and families, handle gifts and loans correctly and use social media safely.
question: A patient's son, grateful for his mother's care, sends a nurse a friend request on social media and offers her £100 'for a night out'. How should the nurse respond?

teach.body: A professional boundary is the line between a caring, therapeutic relationship and a personal one. Code 20.6 says stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries at all times with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past, and with their families and carers. Plain English: you are kind and warm, but you are their nurse, not their friend, partner or business contact, and that holds after discharge too.

teach.caption: Both under-involvement and over-involvement harm the person; the aim is the zone of helpfulness in the middle.

head: Situation
What the Code says
rows: Refuse all but the most trivial (21.1)
Never ask for or accept from anyone in your care or close to them (21.2)
Do not use it to promote causes unrelated to health (21.5)
teach.caption: Accepting more than a trivial gift could be interpreted as an attempt to gain preferential treatment.

teach.h: Social media: the Code applies online
teach.body: Code 20.10: use all forms of spoken, written and digital communication, including social media, responsibly and respect others' privacy. NMC guidance: do not use social networks to build or pursue relationships with patients or service users; do not post pictures of patients without their consent; do not discuss matters relating to people in your care outside clinical settings, even if you think nobody could be identified; and declare any conflict of interest in what you post.
teach.cite: NMC Code 20.10; NMC social media guidance (2025)

rows.label: Images
values: Get consent for any patient image
Post photos of people in your care

rows.label: Work talk
values: Keep patient matters on approved systems
Discuss people in your care online

teach.caption: Posts can be copied and shared beyond your privacy settings; misuse can put registration at risk.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Kofi on a stroke unit
teach.body: Mrs Evans, 82, is discharged home. Her son sends Kofi a friend request and an envelope with £100. Kofi declines the friend request and explains kindly that he keeps patients and families separate from his personal social media. He returns the money, thanking him warmly, because it is more than a trivial gift. The box of chocolates the family leaves for the whole ward is a trivial gift and can be accepted in line with local policy.
teach.cite: NMC Code 20.6, 21.1; NMC social media guidance

teach.h: Warning signs of a boundary crossing
items: Giving one person extra time or favours that others do not get.
Sharing personal problems, phone numbers or social media details.
Keeping secrets with a patient or meeting them outside work.
Feeling you are the only person who understands them.
Discuss any of these with your manager or supervisor early.

children.label: May accept
children.sub: e.g. chocolates for the team; follow local policy

teach.text: The boundary does NOT end at discharge. Code 20.6 covers people who have been in your care in the past, and their families and carers. A 'friend request after discharge' is still a boundary issue.

items: Code 20.6: clear boundaries with current and former patients, families and carers.
Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts; 21.2: never accept loans.
Code 20.7: do not express personal political, religious or moral beliefs inappropriately.
Social media: no patient relationships, no patient images without consent, no discussing people in your care.

summary: You can now recognise when a caring relationship risks crossing a professional boundary, including after discharge. You can also apply the Code's rules on gifts and loans and the NMC's social media guidance to everyday situations.

A.q: A patient being discharged offers a nurse £50 in an envelope as thanks. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept it and share it among the team
Accept it and record it in the gift register
Accept it if the patient insists twice
Thank him and politely decline the money
A.why: Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality, as accepting them could be interpreted as an attempt to gain preferential treatment. Cash is not trivial.

whyNot.0: Sharing the money does not make a cash gift trivial.
whyNot.1: Recording a gift does not make accepting cash appropriate.
whyNot.2: Persistence does not change the nature of the gift.

A.q: Which statement about professional boundaries is consistent with the NMC Code?
options: They apply while the person is still an inpatient
They cover current and former patients and families
They apply to patients themselves but not to carers
They end once the person has been discharged home
A.why: Code 20.6: stay objective and have clear professional boundaries at all times with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past, their families and carers.

whyNot.0: Boundaries extend beyond the inpatient stay.
whyNot.2: Families and carers are expressly included.

A.q: A resident's relative offers to lend a nurse money to help with her car repairs. What does the Code require?
options: Decline the loan
Accept it with a written agreement
Accept it if repaid within a month
Ask the manager to approve it
A.why: Code 21.2: never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them.

whyNot.1: A written agreement does not make a loan from a relative acceptable.
whyNot.2: Quick repayment does not change the prohibition.
whyNot.3: A manager cannot authorise what Code 21.2 prohibits.

B.q: A nurse wants to post a photo from her ward's charity bake sale that shows a patient in the background. What does NMC social media guidance require?
options: Blur the patient's face before posting
Post it if the patient's name is not shown
Get the patient's consent before posting
Post it to a private group of colleagues
B.why: NMC guidance: do not post pictures of patients without their consent, whether or not they could be identified.

whyNot.0: Blurring does not remove the need for consent.
whyNot.1: Leaving out a name does not replace consent.
whyNot.3: A private group still involves posting a patient image without consent.

B.q: Six months after discharge, a former patient messages a mental health nurse asking to meet for a drink. What is the best response?
options: Decline and maintain a professional boundary
Accept, as the patient has been discharged
Accept if they meet in a public place
Accept once the patient's records are closed
B.why: Code 20.6 covers people who have been in your care in the past. The NMC guidance warns against using social networks to build or pursue relationships with patients.

whyNot.1: Discharge does not end the professional boundary.
whyNot.2: Meeting in public is still a personal relationship with a former patient.
whyNot.3: Closing records does not change the boundary duty.

B.q: During a home visit, a nurse is asked by a patient which political party he should vote for. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell him which party she personally supports
Share leaflets for the party she prefers
Advise him to vote as his family suggests
Decline to give her view and refocus on care
B.why: Code 20.7: make sure you do not express your personal beliefs, including political beliefs, to people in an inappropriate way.

whyNot.0: Sharing her political preference with a patient is inappropriate under Code 20.7.
whyNot.2: Steering him towards his family's view undermines his own choice.

C.q: A nurse sees a colleague's public post describing 'a nightmare patient in bed 6' with a photo of the ward. What should she do?
options: Comment publicly asking her to take it down
Raise it with her manager in line with local policy
Screenshot it and send it to the patient's family
Report the colleague to the police straight away
C.why: NMC social media guidance asks registrants to raise concerns about colleagues who misuse social media, through proper channels in line with the raising concerns guidance.

whyNot.0: Public comments spread the post further and are not a proper channel.
whyNot.2: Sharing it with the family spreads confidential information.
whyNot.3: This is a professional concern for the employer, not a police matter.

C.q: A nurse in a care home is close to a resident with no family. She starts visiting him on her days off and gives him her mobile number. What is the most appropriate view of this?
options: Good practice, as it reduces his loneliness
Acceptable if she does not wear uniform
Acceptable as he has capacity and agrees
A boundary concern to discuss with her manager
C.why: Personal contact outside work and sharing personal details are warning signs of a boundary crossing (Code 20.5, 20.6). The nurse should discuss it with her manager so his needs are met safely.

whyNot.0: Loneliness should be addressed through his care plan, not personal relationships.
whyNot.1: Wearing personal clothes does not change the relationship.
whyNot.2: His agreement does not remove her professional duty to keep boundaries.

C.q: A nurse runs a personal blog about her hobby. She wants to sign posts 'RN' and use her registration to support a local planning campaign. Which Code standard is engaged?
options: Code 5.1, respecting privacy in all aspects of care
Code 13.5, completing training before a new role
Code 21.5, using status for causes unrelated to health
Code 23.5, giving your PIN on reasonable request
C.why: Code 21.5: never use your status as a registered professional to promote causes that are not related to health.

whyNot.1: This is not about training for a new role.
whyNot.3: Giving a PIN on request is unrelated to campaigning.

reteach.title: The newspaper test
reteach.question: Would you be comfortable if your manager, the patient's family and the NMC all read about it tomorrow?

blocks.body: Whose needs does this meet: the patient's or mine? Would I do the same for every patient? Would I be happy for my manager to know? If the answer to any of these is uncomfortable, pause and talk to your manager. The same test works online: if you would not say it in the ward corridor, do not post it.

blocks.text: Chocolates left for the whole team are trivial. Cash, vouchers or a personal loan are not, however small the amount seems to the giver.

explain.body: Clear boundaries with current and former patients, their families and carers. Do not take advantage of anyone's vulnerability.

test.q: Which group is NOT expressly covered by the boundary duty in Code 20.6?
options: Former patients
Patients' carers
Off-duty colleagues
Patients' families
test.why: Code 20.6 covers people in your care, those who have been in your care, their families and carers. Relationships with colleagues are covered by other standards.

explain.body: Refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality. Never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or close to them.

test.q: Why does the Code ask nurses to refuse all but the most trivial gifts?
options: Accepting could be seen as seeking preferential treatment
Gifts must be declared to HM Revenue and Customs
Gifts may carry an infection risk on the ward
Gifts are prohibited by the Bribery Act for nurses
test.why: Code 21.1 explains that accepting gifts, favours or hospitality could be interpreted as an attempt to gain preferential treatment.

whyNot.1: Tax is not the reason given in the Code.
whyNot.2: Infection risk is not the Code's reason.
whyNot.3: The Code's stated reason is perceived preferential treatment, not a nurse-specific prohibition.

explain.body: Use social media responsibly. No relationships with patients online, no patient images without consent, no discussing people in your care, declare conflicts of interest.

test.q: A nurse paid by a wound-dressing company posts reviews of its products. What does NMC social media guidance require?
options: Avoid naming any brands in her posts
Declare her conflict of interest
Post the reviews anonymously
Get her manager to approve each post
test.why: NMC guidance: disclose any conflict of interest around material you post on social media, including financial or commercial dealings.

whyNot.0: The issue is the undeclared payment, not brand names.
whyNot.2: Anonymity hides the conflict rather than declaring it.
whyNot.3: Approval does not replace declaring the interest.

explain.body: You can hold any beliefs, but do not express personal political, religious or moral beliefs to people in your care in an inappropriate way.

test.q: A patient asks a nurse to pray with her. The nurse shares the same faith. Which response fits Code 20.7?
options: Refuse, as nurses cannot discuss religion
Encourage other patients to join in
Use the moment to explain her own beliefs
Respond to the patient's request sensitively
test.why: Code 20.7 concerns expressing personal beliefs inappropriately. Responding to a patient-led request sensitively, focused on the patient's needs, is person-centred care.

whyNot.0: Discussing religion is not banned; inappropriate expression of the nurse's own beliefs is the issue.
whyNot.1: Involving other patients imposes on them.
whyNot.2: Promoting her own beliefs shifts the focus from the patient.
